client: I've been really struggling this past week with this big presentation I have coming up at our annual conference. Yesterday during practice I completely blanked — just forgot everything I was supposed to say — and now I can't stop replaying that moment in my head. I'm honestly not sure talking about it is going to fix anything, but I figured I'd try because the anxiety is getting pretty unbearable.
therapist: That sounds genuinely exhausting — having that moment of blanking replay over and over in your mind can make the anxiety feel even bigger than the presentation itself. It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel skeptical about whether talking will help, and I really appreciate that you showed up anyway. Can you tell me a little more about what that replaying looks like — is it more like a fear of it happening again, or more like a harsh inner voice judging you for what happened?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's honestly both, but if I had to pick one that's louder, it's the harsh inner voice. It keeps telling me things like "you've been working there for five years, you should know this material cold — what is wrong with you?" And underneath that is this fear that everyone at the conference is going to see me the same way I saw myself in that moment, just completely falling apart.
therapist: That inner critic sounds incredibly harsh — holding you to a standard of perfection while completely ignoring five years of real experience and competence. What strikes me is that the fear underneath seems to be about being *seen* as falling apart, almost like that one moment would define how everyone sees you. I'm curious — if a colleague you respected had a similar blank moment during practice, would you look at them the way your inner voice is looking at you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: No, honestly I wouldn't — if a colleague blanked during practice I'd probably just think they were nervous and that it happens to everyone. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself it just... doesn't stick. It feels different when it's me, like the rule doesn't apply for some reason and I'm not sure why that is.
therapist: You've just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you'd hold anyone else, and part of you can even see that the logic doesn't quite hold up. I wonder if underneath that "different rule for me" there's something deeper, like a belief that mistakes are more costly *for you specifically*, or that you have more to prove than others do. Does that resonate at all, or does it feel like something else is driving it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That does resonate, actually — there's something about feeling like I don't quite have the same cushion for error that other people do, like I've had to work harder to get where I am and one bad moment could unravel all of that. I think some of it goes back to being one of the few people from my background in this field, and there's always this low hum of feeling like I'm being watched more closely or judged more harshly. It's uncomfortable to say out loud because I'm not even sure if that's really true or if it's just a story I've been telling myself.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage to say out loud, and I want you to know it landed with weight — that experience of carrying more, of feeling like the margin for error is smaller, is something many people in your position know deeply and it's not just a story. I notice you're holding this quite carefully, almost like you're bracing a little even as you say it. Whether or not every moment of being watched is "objectively" true, the toll of living with that low hum of vigilance is very real — so I'm wondering, how long have you been carrying that feeling, and has it shown up in other moments beyond this presentation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think I've been carrying it for as long as I've been in this field, which is over a decade now — it just usually stays in the background and I've gotten good at pushing through it. It's shown up before big meetings, performance reviews, even just speaking up in smaller team discussions sometimes. I guess I never really connected it to the presentation anxiety until just now, and that's a little unsettling to sit with.
therapist: A decade is a long time to carry something mostly alone, and there's something significant about this being the moment it all connects — that kind of realization can feel unsettling precisely because it makes something visible that was easier to manage when it stayed in the background. I notice you seem quite still and quiet as you sit with this, like you're holding it carefully rather than letting it fully land. I just want to gently ask — what does it feel like in your body right now, sitting with that connection for the first time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: There's this heaviness in my chest, like something that's been compressed for a long time is taking up more space than I know what to do with. I also notice I want to kind of intellectualize it and move on quickly — like my brain is already trying to figure out what to "do" with this information rather than just sitting in it. I'm not really used to slowing down enough to feel things this way, and I'm not sure I trust that it's actually useful to do so.
therapist: That impulse to intellectualize is actually your mind trying to protect you — it's been a very reliable tool for getting through hard moments for a long time, so of course it kicks in right now. And yet you noticed it, which tells me part of you is curious about what's on the other side of slowing down, even if it feels unfamiliar and uncertain. I don't think you need to choose between feeling and doing — but I'm wondering, what would it mean for you if it turned out that slowing down like this *was* actually useful?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would mean that I've been making things harder for myself than they needed to be, and that's a strange mix of relieving and kind of grief-inducing at the same time. Like if slowing down actually helps, then what was all that pushing through for — did I put myself through unnecessary suffering? I want to believe it could be useful, but there's also a part of me that's worried if I slow down too much before this presentation, I'll just fall apart completely instead of holding it together.
therapist: What you're describing — that mix of relief and grief — is actually a really healthy and honest response to a genuine realization, and it makes complete sense that both feelings would show up at once. I want to gently offer a reframe to that fear of falling apart: the pushing through hasn't been wasted, it got you here and it's part of you, but slowing down doesn't mean dismantling what holds you together — it might actually mean you're adding something rather than losing something. What if feeling things more fully before the presentation made you *more* steady, not less?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That reframe is interesting and I want to believe it, but I honestly don't have any evidence from my own life that it works that way — every time I've let myself feel things fully before something high-stakes, it's felt like it made me worse, not better. I think what scares me is that I don't have a lot of time before this presentation, and experimenting with a new way of being feels risky when the stakes are this high. How would I even know if I was adding steadiness versus just opening a door I can't close in time?
therapist: Your concern is completely valid, and I want to honor it — this isn't the moment for a big experiment, and I'm not suggesting you overhaul how you operate before Thursday. What I'm actually hearing is that you've built a lot of evidence over time that feeling things leads to falling apart, and that belief makes total sense given your experiences — but I'm curious whether in those past moments, you had any support or tools while you were feeling, or whether you were mostly navigating it alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Mostly alone, if I'm being honest — I don't really have a habit of reaching out when things get hard, and I think I've always seen that as a point of pride more than a problem. But hearing you frame it that way makes me wonder if what I've been calling "falling apart" was actually just what it feels like to carry something too heavy without any help. That's uncomfortable to consider because it means the loneliness has been part of the problem all along, not just a side effect.
therapist: What you just said feels like a really significant shift — reframing "falling apart" as "carrying too much alone" is not a small thing, and I notice there's something tender in how you're holding it, like the words are landing somewhere deep even as you're speaking them calmly. The loneliness being part of the problem, not just a side effect — that's a hard truth, and it takes courage to let it in rather than intellectualize past it. I want to ask gently: what does it feel like to be saying this out loud to someone else, right now, rather than carrying it alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It feels strange in a way I didn't expect — like there's something almost disorienting about being heard without having to immediately justify or defend what I said. I think I've been so used to managing how I come across that just saying something true and having it received quietly is actually harder than I anticipated. And I notice I feel a little exposed right now, which makes me want to wrap it up and move back to the practical stuff about the presentation.
therapist: That impulse to move back to the practical stuff makes complete sense — you've just let something quite vulnerable land, and reaching for the familiar is a natural way to feel safer again. I want to name what just happened though, because it matters: you said something true, it was received, and you didn't fall apart — and that's actually a small piece of evidence that's different from what you expected. We can absolutely talk about the presentation, and I also want to gently hold that what just happened here *is* practical, in its own way.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
